title: Disrupt-then-Reframe
description: A strange opening throws people off balance, making the next, simpler request easier to accept.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: The technique opens with something confusing or unexpected — "these cards cost 300 pennies" — then reframes it plainly: "that's three pounds". The brief confusion interrupts the usual "no", and the reframed ask slips through.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The odd phrasing occupies attention, so the standard resistance script does not run. By the time the meaning lands, the request has already been processed as familiar.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: A fundraiser saying "a box of these is 300 pennies" before asking for three pounds.
An odd opening line in a street pitch that makes you pause and listen.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: The real request arriving immediately after the confusion.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Rarely necessary; clear framing usually serves people better.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Using confusion to lower defences so a request can land before judgment returns.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: You feel briefly disoriented before being asked for something.
Odd phrasing that resolves into a perfectly ordinary request.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: When something confuses you and then a request follows, pause and re-read the ask.
Never agree to something you did not fully understand the first time.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Assuming you misheard rather than being deliberately disrupted.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: Pause when you are thrown off balance.
